t: 3503 – Longest Palindrome After Substring Concatenation I
o: Pick any substring of s and any substring of t (either may be empty) and concatenate; maximize palindrome length. With lengths ≤ 30 there are ≤ 31·30/2 ≈ 465 substrings of each, ~216k combinations — brute-force checking each concatenation is perfectly fine. Single characters guarantee an answer of at least 1. Example 4: "abc" + "ba" = "abcba", length 5.
k: Constraints are tiny: enumerate all substring pairs.
At least one single character always exists, so answer ≥ 1.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over Substring Pairs
a.i: Enumerate every substring a of s and b of t, form a+b, and test the palindrome property by comparing with its reverse.
s: Loop over all (i,j) substrings of s and (p,q) substrings of t.
If concat equals its reverse, update the best length.
a.t: O(n⁴·(n+m)) worst case ≈ 216k pairs × O(60) palindrome check — instant for n,m ≤ 30.

w: Brute force is the right call at these sizes; mention that a smarter O(n³) exists (expand around centers across the seam, plus longest palindromic substring of each string alone) for the Hard version with n up to 1000. Pitfall: remember empty substrings are allowed (but not both empty).
